body: Review by siLLy puPPy — HAIZEA (means "wind" in Basque) is one of the more recognized names when it comes to Spain's late70s progressive folk scene from the Basque region and existed from its formation in Hondarribia in1975 until its demise in 1980. The band released two distinct but vastly different albums duringthat time with this self-titled debut more in sync with the Basque folk revival scene that dominatedthe 1960s while the band's second release "Hontz Gaua" explored more daring experimental excursionsinto the world of electric psychedelic folk with much more complex arrangements. While the bandexperienced quite a few lineup changes during its five year run, amazingly the band's two albumsfeatured mostly the same members including vocalist Amaia Zubiria, guitarist / vocalist Xabier Lasa,bassist Gabriel Barrena and drummer Carlos Busto. This debut would be the only album for guitarist /vocalist Txomin Artola who would be replaced with flautist / guitarist Xabier Iriondo on the band'ssecond album.Prog lovers will probably find little interest in this debut as the band was still very much in thetraditional folk revival stage of the previous decade however with all the Basque musical flavorscorrupted by the experimental commingling of progressive rock and psychedelia imported from abroad,this debut does give a crisp clear glimpse into what the world of unaltered Basque folk actuallysounds like and that would be very similar to a lot of other European folk structures despite theBasque language and culture emerging as an anomaly isolate on a continent long overtaken by Indo-European tribes conquering the Paleolithic cultures. Obvious references on this lead to British folkacts such as The Pentangle or Steeleye Span however Basque folk sounds more similar to Celticflavors from not only Spain but the Breton region of France and of course Ireland, Wales and partsof Scotland. No bagpipes here though!While the second album was a crash course in how to update your traditions in the brave new world,HAIZEA's debut is the polar opposite of keeping things as authentic as possible with gentle folkrock instrumentation, a timeless atmospheric presence with all the tracks heavily rooted in the mosttraditional Basque folk melodies sounding much more like a Smithsonian Folkways release ofhistorical recordings than a so-called modern day progressive band but nonetheless the band performsbeautifully with a light airy feel that finds dual male and female vocals trading off along withgentle acoustic arrangements. While the the instrumentation is almost exclusively acoustic, snippetsof electric guitar do seep in on tracks like "Ura Ixurirk." The most notable different betweenBasque folk music and other European flavors is the strange rhythmic patterns that emerge from theband singing exclusively in Euskera, the native term for the Basque language.While this will not be considered essential for those seeking the more adventurous undertakings ofthe second release, this album is beautifully performed and for lovers of ethnic folk musicalexpressions i can't think of a better place to dive into the little known sounds of Basque folklorethan this debut by HAIZEA. The band's name which means "wind" really does shine though on this debutas the album passes by like a nice gentle breeze near the northern coast where Spain and Francemeet. Although there are few traces of anything progressive or experimental on this one it still isworth exploring simply as a point of reference as to how the Basque folk style was incorporated intothe context of prog rock and psychedelic folk from not only the band's sophomore release but themajority of other bands that were jumping on the progressive bandwagon after the collapse of theFranco dictatorship. The final track "Arrosa Xuriaren Azpian" at ten minutes with psychedelicovertones provides a vital clue to the band's next step. As an ethnic music lover i find this onequite pleasant as music like this is like a time machine that gives a glimpse into the collectivesoul of a culture even though i much prefer the good juicy experimental stuff!

body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if a metronome were forcing its angle further and further outwards...expanding the range until it distorted...the trio, which didn't evoke the image of a trio, begins its second album with "A Visit to Newport Hospital," showcasing organ variations that sound like alarms, red alerts...Dave Stewart combines the magic of the 60s with the mysterious psychedelia that in the 70s would give way to that other Canterbury metric, and Mont Campbell with his measured vocals, plus the organ overlays from which the guiding threads would emerge, the solos of that melody which, as promised at the beginning, were nothing more than alarms of variation on the same note. Jazz and Bossa Nova are implicitly present...staining like raindrops on petals. The alarm awakens us.Contrasong features two tenor saxophones and two trumpets...the monotonous rhythm goes hand in hand with Mont Campbell's singing, and that piano that cuts through Clive Brooks' drums...which cuts through the trumpets...and cuts through the saxophones...and suddenly we're in uncharted territory...like that cover that looks like molten lead, whose solidifying shapes were once used to predict the future... where the trio that did not evoke the image of a trio preferred the mystery of the promise of what it suggests...but is not seen, what is, but is not yet known...an eternal advance, which postpones its realization with the concrete certainty of something that can be heard...can be felt...but not touched, and that when trying to understand it moves away, and comes closer if the mode of perception changes.Boilk is more variations, but in reverse...another way of confirming that intellectual understanding only sets us back...is by not understanding the proposed rules...which are reminiscent of Gy�rgy Ligeti and works like Atmospheres. When, in the final coda, Stewart's other great passion emerges with the Baroque religious organ.Long Piece No. 3 is the album's centerpiece, and here Bach's counterpoints become progressive, slicing through space until they become silence, and then a floating, sidereal space sustained by the drums. Here the trio plays at being a quartet, with the organ's bass lines, leading to an even more ethereal section with the piano...where, from atonal, they could become aggressive, provocative, but always maintaining the tension, that mystery of not knowing what will come next...what note, what chord awaits around the return of the nebula.The second part continues with the variations, the key to the album, creating spacey atmospheres...where that molten lead seems to solidify and take shape...but new suspended melodies, which distanced them from other bands of the genre, anchor them with that Hammond organ with one foot in the 60s, the same as Pink Floyd's Atom Heart Mother, but firm to the pattern that it is the organ that leads the race, this race without a visible final objective.The third part is considered the most complex, alternating between keyboard and piano, with the piano sections being the most virtuosic and classically accomplished. At times, it recalls the darker segments of Emerson, Lake & Palmer's Pictures at an Exhibition.The fourth and final part is even faster, related to Soft Machine's debut, but the jazzy Bossa rhythm with the keyboard cuts and repetitions, plus the bass and the out-of-tune keyboard, end up distancing it and solidifying this experiment of variations as the triumph of melodic harmony in all its forms.

body: Review by The Progolyte — According to ProgArchives, Il Bacio Della Medusa's sophomore album, Discesa Agl'inferi D'un Giovane Amante, is the not only the greatest Rock Progressivo Italiano record of the 21st century, but also one of the greatest progressive rock albums of the 2000s overall (as of writing this, it stands in the top 50 albums between 2000 and 2025). I had incredibly high expectations going into this, because I honestly thought modern rock progressivo italiano couldn't get better than Logos and Unreal City, so I was indeed hoping for a masterpiece. And somehow, it could get better than those. This is hands down the absolute pinnacle of modern Rock Progressivo Italiano and one of the finest pieces in the subgenre. It holds beauty, tragedy, insanity, and power all tied into an imaginative and epic journey. The music found on here is very sophisticated and well crafted, with there being an overwhelming sense of classical influences scattered across the record as the band also pays tribute to the classic Italian bands of the seventies, all with a new twist of horror and stunning visuals the music can put into your mind when listening to it. The entire album consists of 12 individual tracks, but they all function as one continuous composition. The first two tracks, Preludio: Il Trapasso and Confessione D'un Amante, actually have no drums and are more akin to mellow and sometimes even romantic-sounding chamber music, and they do an amazing job at introducing the listener to what music here will sound like and acting as the calm before the storm. From here on out, most of the remaining tracks are just absolutely astounding, and each has a staggering amount of details with incredibly intricate arrangements spliced into every moment. The titles of these pieces are each quite lengthy and depict very vivid pictures about the concept of this record, but in the end the long titles don't bother me when the music here is this good. Numbers like La Bestia Ed Il Delirio, Ricordi Del Supplizio, Nostalgia Pentimento E Rabbia, Sudorazione A Freddo Sotto Il Chiaro Di Luna, and so many other tracks are legitimately some of the strongest Rock Progressivo Italiano I've ever heard, and it's phenomenal the way the band never misses a beat when it comes to keeping the energy and atmosphere going for each one. Each of these and the other ones have everything I could've ever wanted from an Italian album. Raspy vocals, vibrant flutes, intense, unhinged heavy-rocking electric guitars, and even soft and sweet acoustic and classical guitars combined with passionate string work. I really enjoyed how the band balances all the deranged and unpredictable parts with the charmingly quiet yet moody ones. The music is always developing and never stops growing and pushing into different sectors of the story, and it always changes the mood perfectly with the musical direction, and the mind-blowing talent of how these musicians play their instruments throughout the whole is also just the cherry on top for the whole thing. In conclusion, I completely agree with ProgArchives in that this album is truly a remarkable piece of art. Maybe not a completely perfect masterpiece, but definitely a near-perfect masterpiece! Going into this, I knew the album was supposed to be good, but I honestly didn't know it would be THAT good. This is in between a high 4.5/5 and a low 4.75/5 and is a must-listen for any fans of progressive rock, not just of Italian progressive rock. And one more note, this is surprisingly the only Italian album to achieve my "Number 1 album of the year" award, that year being 2008.

This band was formed in the city of Bilbao in 1978 and existed for three yearsin which time it managed to release two progressive folk rock albums beginning with this eponymouslytitled debut which came out in 1979. While one of the mellower bands on the scene, ENBOR (whichseems to mean "tree trunk") featured a rather large lineup which included Joxe Portela (vocals,acoustic guitar), Ram�n Gardeazabal (vocals, acoustic guitar), Manu Urretxaga (vocals, saxophone,clarinet, flute), Amaia Kareaga (vocals), I�aki Arnal (bass, 1978-79), Javi Robador (drums), I�akiGutierrez (vocals, guitar). The band experienced a slightly modified lineup for the second album.Like similarly minded Basque acts, ENBOR also structured its songs around the melodic features ofthe local folk music as well as singing in the Basque language which features a completely differentrhythmic vibe from the Spanish language. The album featured seven tracks and only added up to about33 minutes of playing time. The band delivers a very straightforward style of melodic folk thatfeatured rock instrumentation along with touches of soft jazz. Also typical of the region, ENBOReschewed any of the characteristics of the Rock Andaluz craze that was rocking the rest of Spainduring the late 1970s. The tracks are light and breezy and built around strong melodies and tight-knit vocal harmonies with softer rock attributes such as mid tempos, a folky gentleness and lots ofclarinet, flute and the occasional saxophone presence. While compared to contemporary acts such as Itoiz, Haizea or Oskorri, ENBOR was the leastprogressive of the lot and only featured minor prog elements that were a secondary feature to themusic's main aim of crafting sing-songy folk rock songs. The only time progressive elements areintroduced are in the instrumental parts and then only barely flickering into the prog lite mode.Possible comparisons from other parts of Europe could be made with bands like Mellow Candle,Fairport Convention or the British Folk Revival band only steeped with local Basque flavors ratherthan the more Anglicized styles that found their way into many folk lexicons around Europe. Thealbum is fairly consistent without any surprises to be found. The music exudes a dreamy cloudcovered spring afternoon in some undisclosed woodlands and unlike anything the rather hideous albumcover art may insinuate.Overall it's a pleasant slice of slightly progified Basque folk rock in good taste with no tracksneither sounding lackluster nor particularly memorable. It's just a well presented folk rock stylefrom a nook of the European continent that gives it a touch of an exotic flair given that the Basquelanguage is a true isolate unrelated to any other European language. For those seeking the most progoriented of acts from the region then this one will surely disappoint as the prog characteristicsare rather slim and personally i would barely qualify this album as prog folk at all but it doesfeature a few more elements that would allow it to just squeak by as such. For those seeking themore authentic Basque folk expressions then this one will satisfy on that front as some of theproggier hybrid acts tended to dilute the homegrown flavors in favor of adopting prog aspectsimported from other lands. A beautifully performed album but nothing on here stands out as exemplaryor the least bit essential either.

Their recent albums,however, tend to exhibit a dark and dystopian aesthetic that partially reminisces the music of bandslike Symphony X and Circus Maximus. Furthermore, many of their songs have great commercialpotential, and a large number of the songs appearing on 'The Shadow Theory' make no exception, whichis commendable. This is studio album number twelve from Kamelot, and third overall with Swedishvocalist Tommy Karevik, who has more or less become the face of this new era of the band. His voiceis really powerful, and his range is truly impressive, as heard on this very record.As for the album itself, it is a pretty standard-sounding proggy power metal album that combinesbombastic, pompous keyboards and orchestral arrangements with fast-paced guitars, technical riffs,and a strong propensity for memorable (and sometimes corky) melodies and straightforward songstructures. There is not much separating this album from the rest of the band's albums with Karevikas the lead singer, even though some fans have pointed out that this is not necessarily a bad thing.'The Shadow Theory' is a conceptual record, as the lyrics have a lot to do with sci-fi themes, whichis not uncommon for this band. Some key tracks here include 'RavenLight', 'Amnesiac', 'Static' and'MindFall Remedy', although the majority of the songs on here are well-written and well-produced.There is a melodramatic sheen and an indisputable energy that renders Kamelot's music ratherenjoyable. And with this in mind, 'The Shadow Theory' can be a perfect treat for someone who likestheatrical power metal with proggy bits and contemporary production. I personally find some of thewriting a bit shallow and predictable, as the record hardly introduces any new adjustments to theKamelot formula, but the overall impression I get is that of a really well-composed record.

No (lead vocals, keyboards). I have not always been the biggest fan of their output, but there is no doubt that 2024's 'From Above' was a huge step in the right direction, and here we find them making another change which is massively positive. There are a couple of longer numbers here, but in reality, this release is all about highly melodic songs where crossover sometimes moves into neo, while the harmonies are reminiscent of the softer forms of American AOR.It is an album filled with light and sunshine as the trio continue to progress on the musical journey they commenced in 2018, with this being their fifth album to date, and is a million miles away from the album of covers they released in 2022 of which I was certainly not a fan. This is easy listening prog, but that is not to say it is not worth discovering as there are times when it is nice to move away from the heavy ego of some prog acts and instead turn to something which is middle of the road and still very enjoyable and pleasant on the ears. This style of progressive rock may be too simplistic for some, but I confess I think this has some really good songs, especially when they turn it up and increase the tempo on the likes of "I'll Remember This" as that is a power pop/prog rocker which should be released as a single and aimed at the charts!Lunear continue to delight and surprise, and I wonder what the next album will bring. This is an album where the listener can just have fun and not contort their ears into knots attempting to understand what is going on.

body: Having enjoyed Gimeno’s recent recordings of Bartók (Toronto SO/Harmonia Mundi – review) and Messiaen (Toronto SO/Harmonia Mundi – review), I was keen to hear this new album with the Luxembourg Philharmonic, where Gimeno served as Music Director from 2015–2025. This same artistic team released an all-Dutilleux album in 2024 that included Tout un monde lointain played by Jean-Guihen Queyras. That work, like the concerto on this new release, was written for and premiered by Mstislav Rostropovich. Lutosławski / Bloch Amazon Presto Apple Concerto for Orchestra is the best-known work from Lutosławski‘s early period: the harmonic language is dissonant but tonal, with melodic writing that reflects his study of Polish folksong and the use of older Baroque and Classical forms. The bass drum thwack that opens the Intrada has tremendous impact, signaling a wide and deep soundstage. The layered contrapuntal string entries that follow show Gimeno’s care for textural transparency, though I wanted more snarl from the brass interjections. Indeed, throughout the concerto there were moments where I craved a more garish response from the brass, though the orchestra’s gossamer colors around 5’12” are sensually impressive. The scurrying Capriccio highlights the unanimity of the orchestra’s playing, and Gimeno is sensitive to the darker, mysterious notturno e arioso passages. The Passacaglia has an organic flow and good characterization, though at 16’21” it lacks the driving momentum found in the faster performances by the composer (Polish RSO/Warner Classics); Tortelier (BBC Philharmonic/Chandos); and Dohnányi (Cleveland SO/Decca). The compositional style of the Cello Concerto (1970) is entirely different, the writing far more dissonant (including the use of quarter tones) and contrapuntal. It also features Lutosławski’s aleatoric (sometimes referred to as ‘controlled chaos’) technique. From its inception, the composer claimed it was pure, abstract music, but this has not stopped people (including Rostropovich) from suggesting that the almost constant strife between soloist and orchestra represents the individual’s struggle for freedom within an oppressive political system (a situation which both musicians experienced). The Introduction opens with the soloist’s personal musings around a repeated D, but conflict begins when the cello is chastised by angry trumpets. I must acknowledge that I connect with this music more readily through the unauthorized program; as abstract art, it is less compelling. Rostropovich’s recording, with the Orchestre de Paris conducted by the composer, is an obvious reference performance against which every subsequent release is compared. It is not that every soloist must match Rostropovich’s ‘larger than life’ persona, but there must be a palpable connection with and commitment to this difficult music. I find that in three other readings: Pieter Wispelwey (Netherlands RPO/van Steen/Channel Classics), Paul Watkins (BBC SO/Gardner/Chandos), and Andrzej Bauer (Polish NRSO/Wit/Naxos). Gustavo Gimeno. Photo © Anne Dokter. Wispelwey is especially good at capturing the music’s shifts in atmosphere, and his gorgeous playing in the Cantilena even outshines Rostropovich. Queyras’s technique is beyond reproach, and his reading has plenty of character (as do the orchestra and conductor). Nevertheless, the reading is not as uniquely compelling as those others listed, and both Wit and Gardner inspire greater drama and character from their orchestras. Ernest Bloch‘s Schelomo is based on music originally intended for King Solomon in an unfinished opera, Jezabel. Nicholas Reyland’s liner notes tell us that the cellist Alexandre Barjansky convinced Bloch the cello “could convey Solomon’s meditations ‘just as expressively, if less specifically,’ freeing the depiction from language.” This is sumptuous, emotionally extroverted music. Rostropovich’s reading with Bernstein and the Orchestre National de France (Warner Classics) is considered a classic recording, though I find Bernstein’s effort to wring every ounce of emotion from the performance draws attention away from the music. My favorite performance (also on Warner) features Steven Isserlis, accompanied by the London SO under Richard Hickox. Queyras’ reading is similarly moving, if more inward looking than Isserlis or Sol Gabetta (Orchestre National de Lyon/Slatkin/Sony Classical), and Gimeno ensures that the complexity and richness of the orchestral part is more than mere accompaniment. In short, these are exceptionally fine performances, which nonetheless fail to displace current frontrunners. body: Review by tszirmay — With an album title like that, how could I, the Prog Rogue, possibly resist? This is a strange beast, the van Dam brothers (Niels on lead guitar and Robert on bass) conspire with vocalist Fons Herder and drummer Coen Speelman to be hang around since 1999 and flutter about among the canals and windmills of the Low lands, occasionally recording and releasing this third album after a decade of gazing at the stars (also known as Covid). This is another offering from Bad Promotions, so I am de facto always be open to consider. I must admit from the outset, Rogue Planet has been quite the challenging listen, as the material proposed has some serious ballistic tendencies, skirting on the outer rims of conventional prog, unafraid of flinging harsh riffs that collide with thundering drum exploits, a vocalist who seems to want to explore the softer regions of his lungs.The two- equal part "Few and Far Between" suite opener assuredly establishes the climate for the oncoming onslaught, the Part 1 is suitably turbulent, a windswept gale that can on occasion, can be driven into a frenzy by mother nature's ferocity . Like sitting on a chair on a quiet polder near the Zuiderzee and getting blown into the nearest ditch. Part 2 is the total opposite, a laid-back, blades of the windmill churning leisurely mood, Fons Herder's voice floating like a kite looking for altitude. I can hear the Anathema influences in the symphonic wall-of sound sonorities and the innocuous usage of choir laden choruses that elevate this fine piece into the realm of attraction. Sustaining their striding pace on "Intention", the overall expression conjures impressions of Floydian realms, a floating sheath of reflection on the human condition, its foibles amid oft repetitive failures and the seeming inability to learn how to adapt to realities. Musically, its flowingly attractive. Slight upswing in the chaotic delivery here, the stark guitars grinding with exuberance on "Consequence", spotlighting a deliciously perverse guitar solo that glitters like gold, perfectly imbalanced like an acrobat on a high wire, a thunderstorm on the horizon. The vocal sections are cottony soft with an array of effects, the bass sulky as hell, and a fierce 80s sound to boot, creates quite the stir. I like; I will follow. A sudden silence disrupts the throttling sound, replaced by some showbox rant in a public space about some form of imaginary injustice in order to help consolidate someone's ardent desire to lead the sheep, who knows, its relatively indistinct. Another constricted two-part suite with "Raven Song" and its croaking guitars cawing in the wind, the six strings clinging, clanging and otherwise banging with resolute tremor. The voice remains diaphanous and sweet, yet on Part 2 , it gets flung into that storm I warned about earlier, a threating axis of doomsday mood and mechanical invasion, celebrating some atrocity. Shriek goes the synthesizer, like some warlord in the Arabian desert, the torturing scimitar glowing in the glare. Coen bashes hard, he must be inspired! Yes, finishing off any potential opposition or contrarian opinion, the 9 minute and change the show-stopping "Virgo Calling" closes this fine return to form, certainly more than worthy of being recommended to those who enjoy some edge to their preferred prog razor, the acoustic guitar having the audacity to first soothe the bruised senses with some melancholia, perhaps to confuse or just provide that touch of Dutch psychedelia , you know the redlight district near the poshest hotels and green signed cafes that specialize in more than just java. The sweeping vocals are echoed whooshes that seduce and inspire to dream within a dream, and once the numbness settles in, the greased-up guitars are given their well-deserved liberation, as the swelling chorus keeps rising like the smoke from Krakatoa just before the bang. Wonder where this will be going next?..one never knows with floods, and the Liquid Landscape Dutch know a bit about that.4 Absent globes

body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Another major player in Spain's 1970s Rock Andaluz craze was the Seville based ALAMEDA whichresulted when five likeminded musicians convened at the Conservatory of Sevilla in 1977 or 78(sources don't agree) just in time to catch the flamenco prog craze that was taking the nation bystorm. This band was perhaps the most authentic display of flamenco based prog along with bands likeTriana and Guadalquivir however ALAMEDA was much closer to its flamenco roots with the progaccoutrements used primarily as accents. The band was lucky enough to score a record deal with CBSRecords which led to four highly acclaimed albums released from 1979 to 1983 before the band membersmoved on to other things. This self-titled debut was the first to emerge with its opening track"Aires de Alameda" serving as the band's signature song piece which sets the tone for the band'sshort career of passionate Spanish roots prog.The band featured Pepe Roca (guitar, vocals), brothers Rafael Marinelli (keyboards) and ManoloMarinelli (keyboards), Manolo Rosa (bass) and Luis Moreno (drums). Accusations of being a Trianaclone were rampant because the two bands do indeed rock the flamenco more authentically than themajority of other Rock Andaluz acts. The rumors can be laid to rest though since ALAMEDA's debut wasrecorded before Triana's debut even though it didn't emerge onto the market until after. Forflamenco experts it will be more obvious as well that ALAMEDA's flamenco mining implemented what'scalled buler�as whereas Triana was more focused on rumbas. Add to that ALAMEDA was much more steepedin its flamenco traditions with the prog characteristics as an enhancer whereas Triana was morerooted on the prog side of the equation. ALAMEDA also rocked the zapateado or recognizablepercussive footwork that is common in flamenco. In other words ALAMEDA appears to be the closestthing to pure unadulterated flamenco on the Rock Andaluz scene.What makes this more than pure flamenco though is the use of symphonic synthesized atmospheres andtraces of cool jazz as well as hints of South American folk music from Peru and Chile with perhapsLos Jaivas providing some inspiration in that department. The rock aspects come in with the powerfulelectric bass grooves and keyboard effects although the rock and jazz often blend togetherseamlessly as its more of a fusion style. The vocals are straight out of the flamenco playbook andare directly descended from the tradition. Just listen to any Paco de Lucia album for reference. Thepercussion is divided between the flamenco style and rock drumming which work together quite nicely.The album features seven tracks and a playing time of only just under 34 minutes. The band isconsistent in its delivery throughout with no tracks really standing out except for moments such asthe intro "A La Vera Del Jueves" which begins with a funk jazz keyboard line and a bouncy bassgroove otherwise the flamenco is by far the dominant genre on board.How much you can appreciate ALAMEDA's debut is very dependent on your expectations. If you'reexpecting nerdy prog workouts then look elsewhere although they do exist in small doses mostly tofill in the cracks between beats. This band was not about technical wizardry in the way thatMezquita, G�tic or Iceberg dished out but rather using prog characteristics to enhance the flamencotradition therefore if you're a huge flamenco fan then this band and debut offers an interesting newtwist to the homegrown style that often can sound generic due to its self-imposed limitations. Inaddition to top notch flamenco sounds on board there are plenty of excellent keyboard moments, richatmospheric presentations and more upbeat bass oriented motifs that give much of the album a heavierrock feel. Likewise there are plenty of moments of pure flamenco with the classic acoustic Spanishguitar and homegrown clappers. It's a beautiful album for what it is and one of the few acts thatwould actually find Paco de Lucia playing with albeit on future releases.

body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Spanish pride was high in the 1970s especially after the collapse of the Franco regime and thenation could finally evolve in its own way. While the nation was playing catch up in relation toother advanced European nations, the various ethnic groups that constituted a larger motherlandstill found some sort of respect for the union to a certain degree therefore the push to use theSpanish language in musical forms was very much en vogue much like in neighboring Italy. Despitethis introspection some bands couldn't care less about national identity and went straight for theinternational market. The Seville based THE STORM was one such band to look to the English speakingworld for its inspiration and when it dropped this eponymously titled debut in 1974 got it hailed asthe Spanish version of Deep Purple.This band formed all the way back in 1969 under the name Los Tormentos before christening itselfwith a more Anglicized moniker. The band was a hit on the live circuit hitting the clubs in Madridand Barcelona and attracted the attention of the BASF label with its intricate blend of 70s hardrock with 60s psychedelia and just a touch of prog. In 1974 the band dropped its debut and founditself touring with Queen and although there are zero traces of local Andalusian flamenco flavors onthis release, apparently in the beginning the band did include a few bits to appease the audiences.Surprisingly this was enough to include them as progenitors of the Rock Andaluz scene but in realityon THE STORM's debut there are no incriminating characteristics to peg the band as anything remotelySpanish as the music is right out of the Deep Purple and Atomic Rooster playbook only more steepedin boogie and glam rock of the era. The only Spanish titled song is an instrumental!This album features eight tracks (sang in English) but is quite short clocking in at only about 33minutes. The tracks are more on the pop rock side of the equation however the rowdy bar brawl styleof guitar riffing and massive organ swells give it a touch of that British bravado. Luis Genil doeshis best imitation of Ian Anderson on tracks like "Woman Mine" which also implements a Jon Lordkeyboard style but tracks like the opening "I've Gotta Tell You Mama" and "It's All Right" are muchmore out of The Sweet style of crafting sugary pop hooks fortified with harder rock riffing and inthis band's case a ferocious Hammond organ presence. Every track is quite catchy and although theband does an admirable job of emulating its British counterparts sadly sounds like a second rateimitation as there are none of the technical soloing adventurism that the Purple ones would exhibithowever there are a more off-kilter time signature deviations which is why THE STORM usually getsincluded on prog rock lists and Deep Purple doesn't.Ranging from snappy hard rock anthems with pop friendly hooks or the jazzy instrumental "Un Se�orLlamado Fern�ndez de C�rdoba" or even the more heavy psych jamming style on "Crazy Machine," THESTORM delivered the perfect crossover proto-prog style only given the year 1974 it sounds a bitdated but makes sense considering Spain was still under the dictatorship years at this stage. All inall it's a pleasant album to experience but to my ears many of the anthem rock songs sound a lotlike something KISS would have cranked out in the mid-70s only fortified with Deep Purple-isms. Infact if this band was called Purple KISS it would be more fitting actually. While considered theholy grail of Spanish hard rock of the 70s, for a prog lover this one has very little to offer butwhat puts me off is that it's a bit too close to the bands that influenced it without really findinga unique identity to latch onto. The band would soon disband due to military drafting duties butwould reemerge in the late 70s and pick up where it left off. Best track for prog lovers isdefinitely "Crazy Machine" with its many shifts and musical motifs.

A spaced out symphonic neo-prog odyssey, this record really feels like anatural progression for the band, who are now decidedly exploring these longer pieces of music, inwhich the glowing synths and the spacious guitars of core member Michel St-P�re lay the foundationsfor a richly ornate symphonic rock soundscape, over which the hook-laden prog of Mystery unfoldsbeautifully. With an even stronger emphasis on the "ethereal" side of their music, 'Lies andButterflies' carries several characteristic traits of the modern neo-prog album, in which mood andtexture dominate over pace and complexity. This necessarily makes the album sufficiently enjoyable,but as soothing as the music can be, it often feels pretty linear and monotonous, as if it hadstripped of all the novelty and charisma of some of the band's earlier releases.Key tracks on this 2018 release include the two long suites that bookmark the album. Opener 'Lookingfor Something Else' is a really strong epic that practically explores the main album theme (or theoverall most memorable motif, if you prefer) - a poignant and melodic guitar riff that the banddeveloped into a magnificent prog suite. The closing track 'Chrysalis' is no less exciting - of thetwo big songs, this is definitely the one with the more technical playing. We then have five moretracks in-between the two 16-minute suites, which are quite good as well but barely deviate from thetemplate that we're already familiar with. Put simply, this is an excellent prog album for fans ofmelodic guitars and expansive solos, that should definitely appeal to the ones already familiar withneo-prog. It might not, however, draw in legions of new devotees, and this is a purely objectiveremark, I believe.

body: Review by kev rowland — Like many Yes fans, I still cannot comprehend the band touring without this man at the front as although I love 'Drama' there has been very few Yes albums in the last 40 years worth hearing when he was not there. Mind you, there is also an argument to be had that he needs strong people to work with to produce great results (Jon & Vangelis, Jon & The Band Geeks), and when left to his own devices his solo albums are often not up to nearly the same standards. In many ways this 1997 reissue is at total odds with his 2019 '1000 Hands ? Chapter One' which featured a massive collection of musicians, as for the most part this is just Jon accompanying himself with a few friends here and there (including his wife, Jane).There is some real beauty here in an album which is based on acoustic instruments, folk music and nature, but it is quite inconsistent, and at times it feels almost as if we are trespassing on a private moment when Jon is in a forest clearing, playing his harp to the birds. The result is something which needs to be played on headphones and really listened to as otherwise it just disappears into the aether, yet there is rarely enough substance to truly capture the listener. There will be many who are grateful that Frontiers have again brought it to public attention and finally given it a release on vinyl (as well as CD and digital), but it is not as essential as the likes of 'Olias' and others.
